comments.author: @jasminthomas3528
comments.text: In the 90s through the local church we met a lovely young lady named Zolya. She was part of the church exchange missionary programme. We learnt little bits about Madagascar which was very interesting and sad in some parts about the struggle that the people coped with every day. When the time came for her to return home she gifted my daughter her vali which she still has today. We did keep in touch until she got married to Liva and and had a beautiful baby girl. Sadly we lost touch, even friends visiting Madagascar tried to find her but no luck. I hope wherever they are they are happy and safe. Such a beautiful person. I think because of the island ethnicity I bonded with her as family. The world is no longer this vast unknown place, it's getting smaller and smaller every day as we discover that we have more in common than different.

comments.author: @NICEGLOBE05
comments.text: What truly shines through this documentary is the resilience of the Malagasy people and their deep connection to the land. In Malagasy culture, there's a powerful concept called Fihavanana—a spirit of kinship, mutual help, and harmony with nature. Seeing how communities navigate daily survival while coexisting alongside unique wildlife like lemurs is both humbling and inspiring. Extraordinary storytelling!
